body:
WebHID doesn't have any special handling for the Digitizers usage page, this is probably caused by a Windows limitation:

> In the preceding table, the access mode for input HID clients is *exclusive* to prevent other HID clients from intercepting or receiving global input state when they aren't the target recipient of that input. For security reasons, Raw Input Manager (RIM) opens all such devices exclusively.

> If RIM opens a device in *exclusive* mode, the user can still open a HID device interface without requesting read and write permissions and obtain HID device information via HIDClass support routines (HidD_GetXxx).

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/hid/hid-architecture#hid-clients-supported-in-windows

On Windows, digitizers are only exposed in exclusive mode and are always opened by Raw Input Manager. Chrome's WebHID implementation only tries to open the `GUID_DEVINTERFACE_HID` interface and doesn't check Raw Input API. If the device can't be opened with read-write permissions then Chrome tries again with read-only permissions, then again without read or write permissions. In this case I expect Chrome would fail the first two times and succeed when opening without read or write permissions since RIM already has exclusive access.

The device handle without read or write permissions can't be used to send output reports or receive input reports, but it can be used to get and set feature reports. Perhaps WebHID can open the device through both the `GUID_DEVINTERFACE_HID` and raw input interfaces in order to support all report types.

On the other hand, perhaps digitizers should be explicitly blocked by the [WebHID blocklist](https://github.com/WICG/webhid/blob/main/blocklist.txt). The blocklist already has rules to block access to reports in Generic Desktop Mouse collections, and the reasons for blocking mouse inputs also apply to inputs from other pointing devices like digitizers. Digitizers (and other pointing devices) are sometimes used to enter private information like passwords and PINs that are normally protected and should never be exposed to sites. For instance, a malicious site could abuse access to digitizer input reports to log digitizer inputs when the user is entering their password on a virtual keyboard overlay and convert the pointer coordinates into keystrokes.

In general, we want to discourage applications from using low-level device APIs when there are suitable high-level APIs. It's not clear to me why low level digitizer access is needed and why other APIs like Pointer Events are not sufficient. Can you describe your use case in more detail so we can understand where Pointer Events API falls short?

Thanks for the reply. I already examined the better-known touch and pointer events (e.g. https://patrickhlauke.github.io/touch/), and in my laptop they don't report any rich parameters like pressure/force (other than either 0 or 0.5, depending on whether is clicking) or finger width/height (other than the default 1x1). (Curiously, I also tested two Android phones through Chrome; one reports variable pressure/force but not width/height, while the other reports variable width/height but not pressure/force, complicating interoperability a bit.)

For context, I use an Asus laptop on Windows 11; its touchpad, though ultimately made by Elan, is compatible with the Precision Touchpad protocol (originally for MS Surface laptops, IIRC) and integrates well with Windows in terms of manipulations like smooth scrolling, or many-finger tap actions; things like tap sensitivity and custom actions are configured directly through the OS Settings app, not needing any third-party UI, suggesting the OS is somehow aware about the touchpad. But most applications, incl. Chrome apparently, are fully unaware of the pointing device being a touchpad. Like I said, neither touch nor pointer events within the browser convey anything like analog pressure, etc., much less any advanced parameters like azimuth.

If I had a touchscreen in my laptop, I'm pretty sure more parameters would be reported, even for other applications. But I don't have, and I reckon many other laptop users don't have it too. What I hope that can be eventually possible is using touchpads more or less like a gamepad or joystick (a modern, analog one).

I acknowledge there are security/privacy perils like hooking/logging unrelated events, and I agree there's no way those perils can be ignored. What I propose for most pages is only offering touchpad input capture when the web page is active/focused by every applicable criterion. So if the user is using the same touchpad that is already captured by a page, but now in a different tab or window, the input goes blank for the unrelated page(s).

Very, very few pages would hypothetically need anything more invasive than that, save for some kind of utility application in the future (possibly contained in a platform like Electron). Nowadays there are even APIs like WebUSB (which I personally never needed to use until now), or for controlling system storage and folders; but those kinds of APIs should reasonably be under user permission and promptly revocable by the user.

Edit: maybe this part about security seems confusing the way i wrote. I'll put in simpler terms: As for my purposes, I really don't care if the API reports touchpad input unrelated to my web page (in fact I'd prefer it not to happen, not just because it's unnecessary and confusing, but blocking touchpad in these cases would make for a lighter background app). But as web apps become more powerful, I guess someone will eventually make an app that could process touchpad events even when inactive, for some specific purpose, so I'd recommend also paving way for that possibility, but this is just my speculation.

I wasn't aware of any other HID-directed Windows APIs besides Raw Input API, and I didn't know that Chrome currently doesn't use Raw Input. Now, I checked my existing raw input tests, and not only they don't ask for exclusive access to the digitizer, but they currently can capture the touchpad when inactive (though I blocked this for most of them), and I can even have more than one of them working at the same time, or at the same time that other app receives input like smooth scrolling. Even opening multiple instances of the same app works, as shown in the attached image.

Those experiments (written in C# but ultimately using classic WinAPI) are available in https://bitbucket.org/whateverse/input-tests/src/master/ , in case you want to check; the most complete and interesting one is 'RawInput.Sharp.HidReporterWPF' (the same shown in the picture). I think the binaries are not included there at the moment, but I can also provide them on request.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5ee5fa09-5d3f-4134-ba39-9200898785fd)
Please consider what I wrote and tell me what you think of that. It's been a few days.

Chromium does use Raw Input, but not for WebHID. There's a Raw Input backend for Gamepad API:

https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:device/gamepad/raw_input_data_fetcher_win.h

It would be better if Gamepad shared the same HID backend as WebHID, I'm not sure if that's currently possible or if we are relying on Raw Input for some gamepads. Probably we are, which suggests the HID backend should be updated to support Raw Input.

I'm curious how these devices are exposed on other platforms besides Windows. Are there macOS or Linux limitations on accessing digitizers? In general I feel WebHID should not add artificial limitations except those defined in the blocklist. If a typical app can access it, and there's no justification for blocking it for privacy or security reasons, then the browser should allow it.

That said, I think it's questionable that we block access to other pointing devices but say nothing about digitizers considering these devices are all used to control the system cursor. This issue occurs because Windows treats digitizers the same as mice. Perhaps digitizers were overlooked and we should consider expanding the blocklist. I think it's very likely that even if we did expand support for Raw Input devices we would end up blocking access to the same reports you need for pressure/force, finger width/height, etc. The better solution is to access these fields through a higher level API like Pointer Events, which is already supposed to have this information.

Have you investigated why these values aren't available through Pointer Events? I'm curious about the report descriptor, does it use the standard Digitizer usages? These properties are marked as supported in all browsers, have you checked if they're working in Safari or Firefox? I would guess they're working for some device types (stylus?) and not others.

It looks like Chromium is using [GetPointerTouchInfo](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winuser/nf-winuser-getpointertouchinfo) to read this information ([source](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:ui/views/win/hwnd_message_handler.cc;l=3343;drc=ee15a53a67cfcba92648dfac54a424c2413289fc)), can you test if that API is returning the correct information? If it has the correct info then it must be getting dropped somewhere else and I'd suggest filing a bug against the Chromium>Blink>Input component.

> Are there macOS or Linux limitations on accessing digitizers?

Sorry, I'm not aware about that; I haven't even tried, as I rarely use anything other than Windows. I don't have macOS, and I currently don't develop for Linux yet.

> In general I feel WebHID should not add artificial limitations except those defined in the blocklist. If a typical app can access it, and there's no justification for blocking it for privacy or security reasons, then the browser should allow it.

I understand, although in this case there are real privacy/security issues. But I guess we agree on that already.

> That said, I think it's questionable that we block access to other pointing devices but say nothing about digitizers considering these devices are all used to control the system cursor. This issue occurs because Windows treats digitizers the same as mice.

I must remind that there's already a mouse equivalent to what I have in mind, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Pointer_Lock_API. In fact, since you are evaluating the alternatives, in a way the functionality I requested could be instead added over the Pointer Lock API, but I think this might lead to inconsistencies or exceptional decisions, or even unexpected semantics. A quick search through the text of the just-mentioned MDN article for the strings "touch", "finger" and even "pointer event" revealed me that none of them occur in the article.

> The better solution is to access these fields through a higher level API like Pointer Events, which is already supposed to have this information.

But that's not how touchpads are exposed on Windows. Well, this might change abruptly in the future, I don't know... but it should already be different, and it's not. Notice that even using modern Microsoft-made APIs like WPF, which supposedly respond to touch and even stylus (see my demo 'WinPointerReporterWPF'), the touchpad (at least the one in my machine) only triggers mouse events; and those mouse events, of course, come without finger or pressure data. And this is supposed to be a compatible touchpad, since it uses [Microsoft's own protocol](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/design/component-guidelines/touchpad-implementation-guide)!

> Have you investigated why these values aren't available through Pointer Events?

In a way, it's answered in my previous message (short answer: the OS does not cooperate.)

The 'RawInput.Sharp.HidReporterWPF' demo doesn't really and anything compared to the previous one, except by revealing that the raw data payload in an input report has 14 bytes.

> These properties are marked as supported in all browsers, have you checked if they're working in Safari or Firefox? I would guess they're working for some device types (stylus?) and not others.

You mean touch and pointer events? Firefox seems to behave identically to Chrome on that, treating the touchpad just the same as a mouse. In fact pointer events in both browsers indicate that the pointer type is mouse, with no mouse actually connected. For pointer events' pressure, same thing: either 0 or 0.5 in a digital fashion, but this never reflected the touch or proximity of fingers, it only corresponds to whether the equivalent "mouse button" is down. No touch events are generated here, in any browser.
I never tried Safari but... is it any relevant under Windows? As for stylus devices, I don't have any.

> It looks like Chromium is using [GetPointerTouchInfo](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winuser/nf-winuser-getpointertouchinfo) to read this information ([source](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:ui/views/win/hwnd_message_handler.cc;l=3343;drc=ee15a53a67cfcba92648dfac54a424c2413289fc)), can you test if that API is returning the correct information?

Unfortunately GetPointerTouchInfo doesn't respond to the touchpad. If it did, I guess I'd be using it instead of the Raw Input API.

> UsagePage: 9; ReportID: 4; IsAlias: False; BitField: b11; LinkCollection: 0; LinkUsage: 5; LinkUsagePage: 13; IsRange: False; IsStringRange: False; IsDesignatorRange: False; IsAbsolute: True; HasNull: False; Reserved: 0; BitSize: 8; **ReportCount: 4**; Reserved2: 0-0-0-0-0; UnitsExp: 12; Units: 4097; LogicalMin: 0; LogicalMax: 1; PhysicalMin: 0; PhysicalMax: 65535; UsageMin: 197; UsageMax: 197; DataIndexMin: 8; DataIndexMax: 8; **Usage page: 9; Usage ID: c5**; Values: 17-34-00-00

The 0009:00c5 usage is very unusual, it's a Button usage but is associated with four 8-bit values. The HidReporterWPF demo reads touch width from the first value so this must be the missing touch data, probably width/height for two touch points. I found other Elan touchpad report descriptors with the same 0009:00c5 usage:

https://bz-attachments.freebsd.org/attachment.cgi?id=237365  
https://gist.github.com/ohasanov-hbrw/5a83a7a90059f85041424465bb8dfe3e

I also found https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/design/component-guidelines/touchpad-sample-report-descriptors which gives a sample report descriptor for a Windows-compatible touchpad. The last example "PTP Input Report with Geometry Support" includes touch width and height with the usages 000d:0048 and 000d:0049. I don't see anything that explains 0009:00c5 so I assume it's a vendor-specific thing.

It seems the Asus touchpad driver doesn't support touch geometry even though it supports other PTP features. The device exposes geometry data so I assume this is unintentional. I would suggest checking for driver updates from Asus, maybe this is already fixed.

> The 0009:00c5 usage is very unusual, it's a Button usage but is associated with four 8-bit values. The HidReporterWPF demo reads touch width from the first value so this must be the missing touch data, probably width/height for two touch points.

I understand little about those codes, honestly. You may be right, because empirically here they seem to represent /*finger width and height (I didn't realize about the height when I was making HidReporterWPF)*/ (EDIT: see post below). However, that report only carries data for one finger at a time; and the last 2 bytes always appear as 0 to me.

Those dumps you've shown seem way larger than what I remember having seen. Do you know what tool is used to get them?

> I would suggest checking for driver updates from Asus, maybe this is already fixed.

I checked now, to no avail.

By the way, may I use stuff from your HID Explorer demo in my projects? Especially the huge tables (for vendors, usages and pages).

Man, I'm starting to review those projects from my repository (last time was like 2y ago). By the way, they were based on https://github.com/mfakane/rawinput-sharp, I forgot to mention.

After some new examination of the 0009:00c5 data empirically, I finally figured: the first byte/octet encodes finger pressure; the second byte combines finger width (lower 4 bits) and finger height (higher 4 bits). Strange, since 4-bit values are very low-precision, but that's it. But anyway, I guess Chrome doesn't really need to interpret those data, right? That would be left for the client page, but correct me if I'm wrong.

I also checked the other 5 value usages empirically in my touchpad, and their content matches well with their reported page codes.

> Those dumps you've shown seem way larger than what I remember having seen. Do you know what tool is used to get them?

These are the [HID report descriptors](https://docs.kernel.org/hid/hidintro.html) that describe the device's capabilities, including the layout of all the reports supported by the device. I have some notes [here](https://www.chromium.org/developers/how-tos/file-web-hid-bugs/) that explain how to get the report descriptor on different systems. Windows doesn't expose report descriptors to applications so I think the 

> may I use stuff from your HID Explorer demo in my projects? Especially the huge tables

That was my intent and it's fine with me, but it's best to be careful about licensing. If you need these tables to be properly licensed then I can move HID Explorer to https://github.com/GoogleChromeLabs and add a LICENSE file.

The usage tables are copyrighted by USB Implementers' Forum but the document grants a license to use the tables in products. I think the vendor ID lists are not copyrightable since they are just a list of facts, this might also be true for the usage ID lists since it only includes the name and usage values.

> After some new examination of the 0009:00c5 data empirically

I'd suggest looking at the documentation for the [Elantech Touchpad Driver](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/input/devices/elantech.html) documentation in the Linux kernel docs.

So... pointer events don't respond to touchpads (in Windows at least), GetPointerTouchInfo won't help with that either, and my touchpad is vaguely but not perfectly compatible with the relevant standard... All things said, do you have a resolution or verdict for whether Chrome is going to allow for digitizer report access in WebHID?
